hook: Every LLM call you make travels over HTTP. Auth headers, retries on 429s, pagination, streaming — the client layer decides whether your app is **robust or fragile**.

scenes.title: requests wrote the textbook. **httpx wrote the sequel.**
scenes.sub: One API, two modes: sync and async
scenes.narration: Requests is Python's legendary HTTP library — simple API, huge ecosystem. But it is synchronous only, and in an async world that's a dealbreaker: a requests call inside an async function blocks the entire event loop — PY-10's cardinal sin. httpx is the modern successor: nearly identical API, PLUS first-class async support — same code shape, await added. It also speaks HTTP/2, which some APIs require, and has built-in timeout discipline. Rule for GenAI apps: default to httpx; use requests only in legacy sync scripts. Most official SDKs — OpenAI, Anthropic — already wrap httpx under the hood, so this choice mostly matters when you call APIs directly.

cards.s: The classic · sync-only · blocking inside async code freezes the loop
Same ergonomics · HTTP/2 · strict timeouts by default
awaitable client · the only sane choice inside asyncio · official SDKs wrap it

scenes.narration: The choice that matters most is the third card. Inside any async code — and your GenAI pipelines should be async — only an async client keeps the event loop breathing. httpx gives you one mental model for both worlds: instantiate an AsyncClient for pipelines, a Client for scripts, same method names, same response API. Two httpx specifics worth internalizing: timeouts are NOT optional — httpx enforces a default five-second timeout pool, which surfaces hung-call bugs immediately instead of silently; and connection pooling via a shared client instance reuses sockets across requests, a large latency win versus creating a client per call. Client-per-request is the requests habit you must unlearn.

scenes.title: Bearer tokens, API keys, OAuth — **speak the dialects**
scenes.sub: How credentials ride on HTTP headers
scenes.narration: Three auth dialects cover most GenAI integrations. API keys: usually a custom header — x-api-key — or a query parameter, depending on the provider. Bearer tokens: the Authorization header with the word Bearer and a token — the OpenAI and most LLM APIs' pattern; it's OAuth's token format used directly. OAuth 2: a full handshake — your app exchanges a client-id and secret for a short-lived access token, refreshes it on expiry; use it when acting ON BEHALF of users — 'sign in with Google'-style flows — rather than service-to-service calls. For service-to-service, a long-lived API key or bearer token in an environment variable is the norm. One rule above all: never hardcode secrets — os.environ at minimum, a secrets manager in production.

scenes.title: httpx client with auth, shared across calls
scenes.body:
import os, httpx

# ONE shared client: connection pooling + auth in one place
client = httpx.AsyncClient(
    base_url="https://api.example.com/v1",
    headers={
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['API_KEY']}",
        # "x-api-key": os.environ["API_KEY"],   # dialect B
    },
    timeout=httpx.Timeout(30.0, connect=5.0),  # total 30s, connect 5s
)

async def get_report(id: str) -> dict:
    resp = await client.get(f"/reports/{id}")
    resp.raise_for_status()          # 4xx/5xx → exception, not silent None
    return resp.json()

# OAuth refresh pattern (simplified):
# token = exchange(client_id, secret)          # expires in 3600s
# schedule refresh BEFORE expiry, never mid-call
annot: base_url + relative paths: one client serves every endpoint of an API
raise_for_status() converts HTTP errors into exceptions — silent failures are the real enemy
Two-part timeout: fast-fail on connect, generous on read — 'connected but slow' ≠ 'unreachable'
scenes.narration: The shared-client pattern: auth header configured once, connection pool reused across hundreds of calls, timeouts explicit. Two disciplines shown here. raise-for-status: an un-checked response means a 500-error page flows into your json parser as garbage; exceptions make failures loud and local. The timeout split matters operationally: a connect timeout of five seconds catches dead networks fast, while the read timeout carries the real work — thirty seconds for a heavy report. On OAuth, the production subtlety is refresh timing: refresh on a schedule before expiry — say at eighty percent of lifetime — rather than reacting to 401s mid-call, or every expiry becomes a failed request for some unlucky user.

scenes.title: 429 and 5xx are **transient weather**, not failures
scenes.narration: APIs fail in two families: permanent — 400 bad request, 401 unauthorized, 404 missing — retrying these is pointless and rude; and transient — 429 rate-limited, 500/502/503 server hiccups — these PASS, if you wait. The recipe: retry only transient statuses, with exponential backoff — one second, two, four, eight — capped at a max wait, and add jitter — small randomness — so a fleet of your instances doesn't retry in synchronized waves that hammer the recovering server. Tenacity is the standard library for this in Python: a decorator that encodes exactly these rules. And respect the Retry-After header when present — the server is literally telling you when to come back.

scenes.title: tenacity: the retry recipe, declarative
scenes.body:
import httpx, tenacity

# Retry ONLY transient errors, backoff exponentially, cap the wait
def is_transient(exc: BaseException) -> bool:
    return (isinstance(exc, httpx.HTTPStatusError)
            and exc.response.status_code in (429, 500, 502, 503))

@tenacity.retry(
    retry=tenacity.retry_if_exception(is_transient),
    wait=tenacity.wait_exponential(
        multiplier=1, min=1, max=30) + tenacity.wait_random(0, 1),
    stop=tenacity.stop_after_attempt(5),
    reraise=True,
)
async def call_llm(prompt: str) -> str:
    resp = await client.post("/chat",
                             json={"prompt": prompt})
    resp.raise_for_status()
    return resp.json()["text"]
annot: retry_if_exception gates WHICH failures retry — 401/404 fail immediately
exponential + random jitter: synchronized client retries are how retries become a DDoS
stop_after_attempt bounds total time; combine with PY-10's wait_for for a hard ceiling
scenes.narration: The full recipe in one decorator. Retries only the transient family — the gate is the important part, because retrying a 400 means hammering a server that is correctly rejecting you. Exponential growth respects recovering services; the random jitter is not decoration — if a thousand clients hit a failing endpoint and retry at exactly one, two, four seconds, the retry storm itself keeps the server down; jitter de-synchronizes the herd. Five attempts with a thirty-second cap means worst-case latency is bounded and knowable. Compose with PY-10: tenacity governs the retry rhythm, asyncio-dot-wait-for governs the absolute deadline — together they make 'how bad can it get' a number you can write down.

scenes.title: Big results arrive in pieces — **or one token at a time**
scenes.narration: Pagination: list endpoints return pages, not the whole collection — cursor-based, where the response hands you an opaque next-cursor that you feed into the next request, is the modern pattern, immune to shifting data; offset-based — skip the first N — is simpler but breaks when items are inserted mid-walk. Loop until the cursor is empty. Streaming: LLM responses arrive token-by-token via server-sent events — an HTTP response that never closes, emitting chunks. Why it matters: time-to-first-token drops from twenty seconds to half a second — the user starts reading while the model still thinks. Two consumption modes: iterate chunks for live UX, or accumulate to a full response for downstream processing.

scenes.title: Cursor pagination + SSE token streaming
scenes.body:
async def list_all_users() -> list[dict]:
    users, cursor = [], None
    while True:
        params = {"limit": 100, **({"cursor": cursor} if cursor else {})}
        data = (await client.get("/users", params=params)).json()
        users += data["items"]
        cursor = data.get("next_cursor")   # empty/None → done
        if not cursor:
            return users

async def stream_answer(prompt: str):
    # SSE: response never "finishes" until the model is done
    async with client.stream("POST", "/chat",
                             json={"prompt": prompt}) as resp:
        async for line in resp.aiter_lines():
            if line.startswith("data: "):
                payload = json.loads(line[6:])
                if payload.get("done"):
                    return
                yield payload["token"]   # half-second to first token
annot: Cursor loop: state lives in the response, not your math — insertion-safe unlike offsets
client.stream keeps the connection open and yields chunks — plain .post would buffer everything
the 'data: ' prefix is the SSE protocol — parse, don't split naively on newlines
scenes.narration: Both patterns shown side by side because they share one idea: HTTP as a FLOW, not a snapshot. Pagination walks a cursor until the API says done — never compute offsets yourself; the cursor is opaque for a reason, and branching data makes offset math wrong. Streaming via client-dot-stream and aiter-lines: the connection stays open, each server-sent event line arrives as it's produced. The protocol detail — events prefixed with 'data colon space' — matters because blank lines are keepalive heartbeats, not content; parse with the prefix check, not naive splitting. FastAPI can EMIT SSE just as easily — PY-13 covers that — completing the loop: your app streams from the LLM and streams to the browser, end to end.

scenes.title: Clients mastered. Time to BE the server.

recap: httpx for everything new: one API for sync and async, HTTP/2, enforced timeouts — requests blocks the event loop
Auth dialects: x-api-key, Bearer tokens, full OAuth for user-delegation; secrets from env, never code
Retry only transient statuses with exponential backoff + jitter; paginate via opaque cursors; stream LLM tokens with client.stream for instant UX

quiz.q: Why is requests a liability inside async code?
opts: It's synchronous — a blocking call freezes the entire event loop until the response arrives
quiz.why: The event loop's power is doing other work while waiting; a blocking client wastes every other coroutine's time.

quiz.q: Which failures should a retry policy retry?
opts: Only transient ones — 429/5xx — with exponential backoff and jitter; 4xx client errors fail immediately
quiz.why: Retrying permanent errors hammers a correctly-rejecting server; jitter prevents synchronized retry storms.

quiz.q: Why prefer cursor pagination over offset pagination for changing data?
opts: Offsets break when items are inserted/deleted mid-walk (you skip or repeat rows); cursors are insertion-stable by design
quiz.why: The cursor is an opaque bookmark into the server's ordering — your page math can't be invalidated by inserts.

code.title: The resilient LLM client, assembled
code.body:
import os, httpx, tenacity

client = httpx.AsyncClient(
    base_url="https://api.llm-provider.com/v1",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['LLM_KEY']}"},
    timeout=httpx.Timeout(60.0, connect=5.0),
    limits=httpx.Limits(max_connections=100),  # pool cap
)

def transient(e: BaseException) -> bool:
    return isinstance(e, httpx.HTTPStatusError) \
        and e.response.status_code in (429, 500, 502, 503)

@tenacity.retry(retry=tenacity.retry_if_exception(transient),
                wait=tenacity.wait_exponential(1, max=30)
                     + tenacity.wait_random(0, 1),
                stop=tenacity.stop_after_attempt(5), reraise=True)
async def complete(prompt: str) -> str:
    r = await client.post("/chat", json={"prompt": prompt})
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()["text"]

async def complete_stream(prompt: str):
    async with client.stream("POST", "/chat",
                             json={"prompt": prompt}) as r:
        async for line in r.aiter_lines():
            if line.startswith("data: ") and line != "data: [DONE]":
                yield json.loads(line[6:])["token"]

# One client, two personalities: buffered complete + live stream
annot: max_connections caps the pool — combined with PY-10's semaphore, backpressure has two gates
One shared client = one auth config, one pool, one timeout policy — consistency by construction
complete_stream is the production UX path: first token in <1s beats 'complete' in 20s every time

notes:
# HTTP Clients

## requests vs httpx
- requests: sync-only → blocks event loops. Legacy scripts only.
- httpx: same API, sync + async, HTTP/2, strict default timeouts.
- Shared client instance: connection pooling; never client-per-request.

## Auth
- Dialects: `x-api-key` header · `Authorization: Bearer` · OAuth2 (user-delegation flows).
- Service-to-service: env-var key/bearer. Never hardcode; secrets manager in prod.
- `raise_for_status()` everywhere — silent failures are worse than crashes.

## Retries
- Transient only: 429, 500/502/503. 4xx fails fast.
- Exponential backoff + jitter; respect Retry-After; cap attempts; tenacity.

## Pagination & streaming
- Cursor-based (opaque next_cursor) > offset for changing data.
- SSE via `client.stream` + `aiter_lines()`; parse `data: ` prefix; blank lines are heartbeats.
- Streaming = sub-second time-to-first-token UX.
